# Decoding P0420 in a Prius: Oxygen Sensors and Catalytic Converter Failure

When a 2005 Prius throws a P0420 code, the immediate assumption is often a dead catalytic converter. However, diagnosing this issue requires distinguishing between actual catalyst failure and sensor degradation. The owner of the vehicle in question utilized a smartphone scan tool to visualize fuel/air commanded equivalence ratios, revealing behaviors that complicate the standard diagnostic flow.

### Understanding the O2 Sensor Plots

The core of the diagnosis lies in interpreting the lambda readings from the upstream (front) and downstream (rear) oxygen sensors. Under normal operating conditions, the engine control unit (ECU) keeps the mixture oscillating rich and lean to maintain stoichiometry. This results in an upstream sensor voltage that fluctuates rapidly between 0.1V and 0.9V.

The plot from coasting down shows a chaotic response when the engine restarts. When the Prius enters EV mode while coasting, the internal combustion engine stops, cutting off fuel injection. Consequently, the upstream oxygen sensor is deprived of exhaust flow and effectively "starves" until the engine cranks back up. Once the ECU resumes fuel injection, both sensors experience a massive transient spike in voltage as they attempt to re-acclimate to the new air-fuel ratio. This behavior, while alarming on a graph, is technically expected during the transition from EV mode to combustion mode and does not necessarily indicate a faulty component.

However, the second scenario presents a clearer picture of system health. When the vehicle is running under load (foot off throttle, then accelerating), the upstream sensor continues its normal high-frequency oscillation. The critical diagnostic metric here is the downstream sensor. In a healthy catalytic converter, the three-way catalyst acts as a buffer, smoothing out these fluctuations and keeping the downstream voltage relatively steady. If the rear sensor begins to mimic the "wobbly" behavior of the front sensorâmoving up and down in sync with the rich/lean cyclesâit indicates that the catalyst is no longer storing oxygen or reducing emissions effectively.

### The Lambda Voltage Discrepancy

The owner noted that their readings centered around 1V rather than the expected ~0.7V. This observation highlights a common pitfall when using aftermarket diagnostic tools. Many OBD-II scanners sample the raw analog voltage before the ECU applies its specific scaling algorithms. While standard wideband sensors operate in a different range (0 to 5V), narrowband zirconia sensors typically switch between low and high states around 0.45V.

If your scan tool displays voltages consistently higher than expected, it could be a calibration issue within the Dash Command software or a misunderstanding of the raw data versus the processed lambda value. Before assuming hardware failure, verify if the tool allows you to toggle between raw voltage and calculated lambda. If the tool is misinterpreting the signal baseline, the visual "noise" in your plots might be exaggerated, leading to a false diagnosis of converter efficiency loss.

### Addressing Underlying Causes at 170,000 Miles

The owner eventually concluded that the rear sensor was bouncing with the forward sensor's lambda reading after rescanning and ruling out vacuum leaks. They decided to replace the catalytic converter. This decision aligns with standard practice: if there is no exhaust leak upstream of the catalyst and the downstream sensor mirrors the upstream behavior, the converter has likely lost its chemical efficiency.

However, replacing the part does not guarantee a permanent fix if an underlying condition exists. At 170,000 miles, the vehicle has surpassed typical service life expectations. Common culprits for premature catalyst failure include oil consumption (burning oil fouls the catalyst) or rich-running conditions caused by a failing fuel injector or MAF sensor. Even with a new converter, these issues can quickly degrade efficiency again.

While "cat cleaner" additives are often marketed as a remedy, they rarely address physical breakdown of the ceramic substrate or melted platinum groups. If the decision is to replace the unit yourself, ensure you inspect the wiring harness for heat damage and verify that no exhaust leaks are present before clearing the code. Clearing the code and passing an EVAP test is only the first step; the drive cycle must complete long enough for the ECU to re-run its continuous monitor and confirm the new converter's efficiency.
